speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: We have a world-class judiciary that is known for its competence, independence and utmost integrity.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: The sound justice system has brought about many tangible benefits to Singaporeans.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: The value of our legal industry and jobs in the legal sector have grown in tandem with our status as a legal hub.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: A reputation for being an efficient dispute resolution centre and respect for the rule of law have also enhanced Singapore's attractiveness as an investment destination.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: But we cannot afford to rest on our laurels.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: We have to constantly look ahead and improve on what we have to stay relevant and competitive.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: So, this Bill represents the latest of our continual efforts to improve our justice system.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: First, I would like to touch on the digital transformation of the Courts.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: As Members will appreciate, the COVID-19 pandemic has necessitated a reduction in the level of person-to-person contact.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Under the Bill, Courts will be generally empowered to conduct hearings remotely, using appropriate electronic means such as video-link.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: For example, we may have hearings where one party is physically present before the Judge while the other party appears via video-link.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: We may also have hearings that take place entirely online.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Regardless of the specific remote hearing arrangements, the Court's overriding duty in each case will be to ensure that proceedings are conducted fairly to all parties.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: There will also be statutory powers to exclude certain types of matters from being heard remotely, should this prove necessary.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Where witness testimony is concerned, the Courts have existing powers under the Evidence Act to allow witnesses to give evidence remotely in civil matters.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: The Bill will now amend the Evidence Act to enhance safeguards relating to remote testimony.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: For example, matters which the Court must consider before it allows witnesses to give evidence remotely can be prescribed.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: For criminal matters, the Courts already have existing powers under the Criminal Procedure Code to allow a witness to give evidence via video-link if the witness is in Singapore.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: The Bill seeks to expand this in two ways.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: There will, of course, be appropriate safeguards for this.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: For example, in the case of a witness of fact, all parties, including the defence, must agree to the witness giving evidence from outside Singapore.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Where parties do not agree, the witness will only be allowed to do so if he is unable to give evidence in Singapore and has set out in writing the evidence which he proposes to give to the Court.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: This provides advance notice to the other parties so that the veracity of the witness' evidence can be adequately investigated.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: The Court may also allow an accused person to appear or give evidence via live video-link from another place in Singapore if all parties agree.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: In both cases, the Court must be satisfied that allowing the witness or the accused person to give evidence remotely will be in the interests of justice.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: The Court must also be satisfied that there are sufficient administrative and technical arrangements in place in order to facilitate the taking of evidence.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: For proceedings relating to contempt of court, a framework similar to that in the CPC will be introduced.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: The Bill will also empower the Courts to decide any matter based on written submissions and documents tendered by the parties, without any oral hearing.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: This is commonly known as a "paper hearing".

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: A paper hearing can improve efficiency in the conduct of administrative pre-trial matters and can also save time and costs when it comes to the disposal of substantive matters that are document-centric.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Appeals can also be heard on paper where appropriate.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: The Bill will also make clear that parties can address the Court and make their arguments via an "asynchronous" exchange in appropriate cases.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: The intention is also to adopt, what we call an “omni-channel” approach.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: So, lawyers and judges will be able to log in to the e-Litigation system or use the new SG-Courts application to communicate with the Court.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: They will be able to give information to the Court such as the number and availability of witnesses, or other pre-trial preparatory matters, whilst they are “on the go” and from remote places.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: This would also reduce the need for litigants, lawyers and the Court to schedule fixed timeslots when they must all appear together at the same time and at the same location to deal with a matter.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: This will bring about increased convenience and improved productivity.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Overall, the amendments will empower our Courts to conduct their proceedings in a flexible manner, through the use of technology.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: However, technology is but a means to an end.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: The foremost consideration for the Court in all cases will be to ensure that the proceedings are conducted fairly for the parties, including, and perhaps, in particular, for litigants-in-person, and that justice is done.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: In considering what a suitable mode of hearing might be in each case, the Court may consider matters such as whether the case is a civil or criminal one, the complexity of the case and the kind of and the degree of fact-finding that might be required in each case.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: The stage of proceedings would also be an important consideration.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: For example, the Court may consider it appropriate to deal with administrative pre-trial matters via an asynchronous hearing.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: The Court may also decide that certain interlocutory issues can be dealt with on paper but may direct parties to appear in-person when it comes to other matters.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Litigants-in-person who find it difficult to cope with technology can also request for an in-person hearing and make their reasons known to the judge.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: First, related amendments to the Administration of Justice Protection (AOJP) Act.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Therefore, unauthorised recordings of court proceedings which are conducted by electronic means, or publication or transmission of such proceedings, will constitute contempt of court.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: This will safeguard the sanctity of remote hearings in the same manner as physical hearings.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: In other words, what you could otherwise not have recorded or transmitted in a physical setting in court, you cannot also do in a remote, online court proceeding.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Next, the Bill also introduces amendments to modernise and simplify court terminology.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: The aim is to make it easier for court users and the general public, who are not legally trained, to understand our laws and Court practices without the jargon.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: If the Court is not satisfied that parties have made efforts on this front, the Court will be empowered to order parties to attempt amicable resolution before continuing with litigation.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: The learned Chief Justice, in a 2019 speech, said that there is a need to challenge the longstanding assumption that disputes are inherently confrontational and therefore, solutions must also be adversarial in nature.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: The Chief Justice opined and I agree, that justice must be more than the enforcement of legal rights and obligations.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Justice can also be about the maintenance of peace and the promotion of compromise, conciliation and closure between parties.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: As a litigator myself for many years, I agree with the Chief Justice’s observation that maintaining relationships is sometimes even more valuable than vindicating one’s legal rights in court.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: This amendment will, therefore, give force to that exhortation and will hasten a shift in mindset as to how justice may be achieved by focusing on the common interests of the litigants and reaching common ground through mutual agreement and compromise.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: This statutory framework is based on the well-established role of the AG as the guardian of the public interest.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: The AG has a right and a duty to represent and safeguard the public interest.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: The AG does not intervene in court proceedings with a view to advancing the interests of any litigant.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Rather, the AG intervenes to represent the public interest and to place before the Court, a non-partisan perspective on public interest issues.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: This strengthens the integrity of proceedings before the Court, especially in cases where the Court's decision may have ramifications on the wider public good.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: First, the AG may apply to the Court for permission to intervene in any court proceeding, if he is of the opinion that the proceedings raise a question of public interest and the intervention is necessary in the public interest.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: To be clear, this will not affect the AG’s right to intervene in court proceedings under any other written law.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: If the Court is satisfied that the AG has adequately set out the reasons in support of the application, then the AG is made a party to the proceedings.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: In deciding whether to grant permission, the Court does not at that stage enquire into the merits of the AG’s application or opinion.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: An existing party to the proceedings may still apply thereafter to set aside the intervention on the basis that this would be in the interests of justice.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: But pending the resolution of the setting aside application, the AG remains a party to the proceedings.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: This ensures that proceedings do not come to a standstill once an application to set aside is made.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: The Court has the power to order costs for or against the AG, as it thinks fit.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Overall, the amendments in the framework that I have just outlined will provide greater clarity to the process for the AG to intervene in court proceedings and also minimise uncertainty and satellite litigation.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: This is commonly known as a "freestanding interim relief".

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Under these amendments, the General Division may grant any type of interim relief which it has the power to grant, in proceedings within its own jurisdiction.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: In other words, the Court is circumscribed by the power it already has within its jurisdiction to grant in those proceedings.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: For example, a Mareva injunction, which is quite typical, or a search order or an Anton Piller order.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: However, warrants for the arrest of property and provision for obtaining evidence are excluded.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: The amendments are consistent with the approach in the UK and Hong Kong, and will support our efforts to promote Singapore as a leading international dispute resolution hub.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: At present, the Court of Appeal and the Appellate Division have powers to summarily dismiss unmeritorious appeals.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: To avoid doubt, the Courts have the ability to exercise their powers of summary dismissal without hearing oral arguments.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: The summary dismissal powers are narrowly scoped and are intended to manage frivolous appeals that are a drain on judicial resources.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: We have also provided that the Court must consider representations made by the appellant and must also give the appellant a reasonable opportunity to show cause, before exercising its summary dismissal powers.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: First, to make drafting changes and align the phrasing of the summary dismissal provision for the Family Court at clause 25 of the Bill with the equivalent provisions that apply to the General Division and to the State Courts.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: These provisions are intended to have the same effect.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Second, to ensure that the Court has the power to summarily dismiss certain unmeritorious criminal applications on its own motion.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: For example, these could be applications brought without any sufficient ground or where in a particular case where the Court has no jurisdiction.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: This power will apply to criminal matters, such as an application for criminal revision or a criminal motion, where the existing summary dismissal provisions in the Criminal Procedure Code do not currently apply.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: We will align the position across all the Courts for Agreements not to Appeal by introducing a clear and simple framework that the parties may use to restrict their right of appeal.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: This already exists to some extent in the State Courts Act and the Family Justice Act today.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Under these amendments, Agreements not to Appeal must be in writing and signed by or on behalf of all parties.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: This ensures that parties' attention is drawn to the implications of their agreement and minimises ensuing satellite litigation over whether there was in fact an agreement or not.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Third, flexibility in the size of the coram.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Currently, proceedings in the General Division are usually disposed of by a single Judge.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: This may be the case where, for example, there are novel or important questions affecting the public interest, which could benefit from the collective wisdom and insight of a larger coram.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Proceedings under the Arbitration Act and International Arbitration Act.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Today, proceedings under the current Arbitration and the International Arbitration Act, are heard in open court by default, unless a party applies for the matter to be heard otherwise than in open court, in camera, for instance.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: We have considered feedback from various stakeholders, practitioners, that as a matter of practice, it will be common for parties involved in proceedings, involving arbitration, such as in those two Acts, to make applications, for the matter to be heard in private.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: The Bill also implements the recommendations of the Civil Justice Commission and the Civil Justice Review Committee.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: In addition to these, however, there are proposed amendments to the Attorney-General (Additional Functions) Act.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: I seek clarification on Part 4 of the proposed Bill.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: In MinLaw's factsheet on the technical amendments to this Bill, the objective is to, "clarify the scope of the Attorney-General's right to intervene".

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: I have some questions on this part, as I alluded to earlier.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: I will first summarise the proposed amendments in Part 4, then discuss the current position in Singapore law and finally, briefly compare Singapore's position with those and other common law countries.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: The Bill proposes a statutory framework for the Attorney-General, or AG, to intervene in proceedings where the AG is of the opinion that the question of public interest has arisen and the AG is of the opinion that it is necessary to place information or make submissions before the Court.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: The Court is only to look at whether the grounds for intervention are adequately set out with a supporting affidavit.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: So, although the proposed amendment say that the AG must apply for permission to intervene, in reality, there would be very little room for the Court to deny certain application.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: If the existing parties to the proceedings disagree with the AG's intervention, the proposed amendments place the onus on those existing parties to apply to set aside the permission to intervene after it has been granted to the AG.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: The changes proposed by this Bill are extended to all civil proceedings.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: The proposed clause 4A(3) allows the AG to intervene in any proceedings and I emphasise the word "any".

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: They are not criminal proceedings and are proceedings to which the AG is not a party or representing any party.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Clause 4A(4) spells out that the AG may intervene in proceedings such as judicial reviews, any civil proceedings, family proceedings or quasi-criminal proceedings appeals and proceedings before Judges under the Legal Profession Act and the Medical Registration Act, although clause 4A(4) is careful to point out that this list does not limit subsection 3, which as I have said, allows intervention in any proceedings.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: However, in a private law dispute, the Bill before us today would allow the AG to intervene, with the Courts having no scope to assess the merits of the AG's submission as to what public interest the AG is protecting and in the event an application is made, to set aside the order granting permission for the AG to intervene.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Can the Minister confirm that these amendments effectively represent a significant shift or a shift to the common law position on the AG's right to intervene?

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: There is already a process under common law for the AG to apply to intervene and for the Courts to consider the merits of the AG's application.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: It is a well-established procedure and there is no case law in Singapore to suggest that the AG is fettered from intervening in the public interest.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Quite simply, the current intervention process under common law appears to work well.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: In Singapore, the AG may currently intervene through the authority of legislation or via common law.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: First, the AG has the right to intervene where a statutory right is given.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: For example, section 46 of the Charities Act entitles the AG to be heard in appeals to the High Court against decisions of the Commissioner of Charities.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Other statutes that give the AG the right to intervene in specific situations are the Industrial Relations Act and the Women's Charter.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Second, the AG may also intervene at common law, as I intimated earlier.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: This process can be seen in action in the cases of Deepak Sharma v Law Society of Singapore and ARW v Comptroller of Income Tax, both of which are referred to in the Explanatory Statement.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: In the ARW case, the High Court Judge stated in his judgment in 2017 that an intervener must establish his standing.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: He said that in public law matters, the standing of the AG to intervene is not usually in question but that in a civil suit based on private law rights, the AG's role may not be immediately apparent and must be properly established.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: From what the Judge said, it does seem clear that, conceptually, at least, a distinction is currently made between matters of public law and private law.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: In matters of private law such as in Deepak Sharma and ARW, the AG currently has to justify his application to intervene and the Court decides on the merit of the application.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: For other types of cases, the Australian AG can seek leave from the court to intervene.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: The AG has the right to intervene in proceedings affecting the Crown's rights, property or profits.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Otherwise, the AG must seek leave from the court to intervene in other cases.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: These positions are broadly similar to Singapore's current position.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Distinction is drawn between public law cases and private law cases, even those private law cases that may involve the public interest.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: More specifically, I would like to ask the Minister the following questions.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Number two: are there possible cases which have not occurred in the past, which the Government is preparing for as a contingency?

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: And if so, what are these possible scenarios?

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Number four: how actively is the AG looking to be in applying these proposed amendments.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Thanks to the efforts of MinLaw, led by the hon Minister Edwin Tong, which launched the Legal Industry Technology and Innovation Roadmap in October 2020, law firms are supported in their endeavour to develop legal tech solutions, manage and mitigate risks that come with increasing digitalisation and benefit from the eCourt model, which has enhanced functions such as system integration, speech to text technology and leverages on AI.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: The Courts transformed quickly to regain lost ground in terms of lost hearing days arising from the circuit breaker in April and May last year when it pivoted to remote hearings.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: I have attended numerous virtual Court hearings and online dispute resolutions as counsel.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: The productivity gains and cost savings arising from the usage of digital platforms are significant and acknowledged by all Court users.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Hearings nowadays are also more focused in that the parties would have made full written submissions and the Courts, at all levels, would generally take the lead in asking pointed questions of counsel before making decisions.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: All these translates to efficiencies in the administration of justice and provides litigants with higher value.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: This will ensure that these hard-won costs savings and productivity gains will endure beyond the pandemic.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: The hon Chief Justice in his address in the Opening of the Legal Year this year sounded a cautionary note on the impact of technology on such persons.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: He said, "As we embrace and explore the greater use of technology, we must remain keenly sensitive to the needs of Court users who are less technologically equipped or inclined and ensure that technology is an enabler rather than an impediment." In light of the Chief Justice's observations, may I please ask what measures will be put in place to help LIPs so that the interests of justice would be met?

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: The hon Minister did mention that the raison d'etre of Court proceedings would be to ensure fairness.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Clearly, at one level, the remote hearing requirement can be waived for LIPs.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: But I am just wondering whether there could be avenues for LIPs to learn how to have access to remote hearings, how to use the remote hearing functions or even draft submissions for paper hearings.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Another associated question I have is with respect to the intention to allow accused persons to appear and give evidence remotely from prisons.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: I now move to my second point on the matter of the AG's right to intervene in Civil Court proceedings.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: I note that the provisions dealing with the right is premised on the standing of the AG as a guardian of public interest under common law.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: This standing does not stem from the duties of the Attorney-General as set out in article 35 of the Constitution.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: I am aware that the AG's standing as the guardian has been recognised by the Court of Appeal on several occasions.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Notwithstanding that, it seems to me desirable that the AG' role as the guardian of public interest should be codified in our Constitution.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: As acknowledged by the Court of Appeal, the AG's office is a high constitutional office equal in status to the judiciary.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: His power over prosecution stems from a constitutional grant under article 35(8) of the Constitution.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: His role as the Government's legal adviser is also constitutionally entrenched.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: It is also important to entrench his role as the guardian of public interest so that whatever steps he may take to safeguard public interest in civil proceedings is derived from an exercise of a power that is not only independent but constitutionally protected.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: In this way, his power cannot be trumped by ordinary legislation.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: My other questions are on the mechanics of the two-step procedure that is being contemplated when the Attorney-General applies to intervene.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: In this regard, I heard the hon Leader of the Opposition mention that the power of intervention is based on common law.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Based on my understanding, that is not the case.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Under common law, the AG's position as the guardian of public interest is established.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: But as far as the powers of intervention are concerned, they are provided for under the rules of the Court and in particular, Order 15.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: In the event the Court allows the AG's application, then at the second instance, parties may apply to set aside the intervention.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: As the hon Minister who spent a lot of time in private practice would be aware, such responsibility is usually assumed by litigants making Court applications without notice and to some extent, it may address some of the concerns expressed by the hon Leader of the Opposition as well.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: On the twin threshold questions of (a) whether a question of public interest has arisen and (b) whether it is necessary in the public interest for the AG to intervene, I seek clarification as to what is meant by the words "has arisen".

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Sometimes, public interest issues may be not part of the key issues as framed by the private parties to the proceedings.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: There could also be a situation, as was discussed in the Court of Appeal case of ARW v Comptroller of Income Tax, where the core decision of the Court may not trigger a public interest issue although the issue may have been discussed but not perhaps being germane for the disposal of the case.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: And in this regard, I will say that it is not unusual for AGs to apply to intervene in civil proceedings because there could be situations where, for example, in my own experience, documents may be sought and these documents may be something that is subject to state immunity.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: And in those circumstances, in safeguarding public interests, sometimes, the AG may wish to intervene.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: So, from my own experience, it is not unusual.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: My two points may appear separate, but they are in fact, intertwined.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: This speaks to the principle of fairness as put by the hon Minister.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: I welcome the hon Minister's views on my suggestions.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: The Courts have shown remarkable resilience in this pandemic, adapting to ensure that the judicial system remains open to users and that justice is both done and seen to be done.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: I have three points of clarification to make.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: First, I seek clarification on the Court's new power to order parties to attempt amicable resolution in civil proceedings.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Amicable resolution, such as negotiation and mediation, work best when parties participate in good faith.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: This point is underscored in the Rules of the Court.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: In such cases, the process is no longer voluntary and it raises four sets of questions about effectiveness and implementation.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: One, has the Ministry studied what cases are amenable to amicable resolution?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Clarity on such situations will help the Court decide on what circumstances to order an attempt at an amicable resolution.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Two, what constitutes an attempt at amicable resolution?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Will there be clear requirements to verify such attempts?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: For instance, it may be useful to require that parties attempting mediation go through an accredited mediator.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Three, how will the Court ensure that parties participate with good faith in attempts at amicable resolution?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: I can imagine a bad-faith party relying on the Court's order of amicable resolution as a strategic manoeuvre by parties to prolong litigation and financially wear down opponents.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Four, will there be consequences of non-compliance with such an order?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: The Minister's answers to these questions will help ensure that Court orders for amicable resolution do not get undermined by bad-faith actors.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: The immunity is limited to actions done in good faith and without any fraud or wilful misconduct.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: This appears to mirror section 68(4) of the State Courts Act, which provides similar protections for judicial officers and Court-appointed mediators for alternative dispute resolution in the State Courts.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Alternative resolution processes, such as mediation and conciliation require different skills from hearing a case as an adjudicator.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: These specialised skills are honed by professional mediators and conciliators over years of training and experience.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: For this reason, judicial officers in the State Courts are required to undergo basic training in mediation.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Will there be a minimum requirement that officers and mediators at both State Courts and Supreme Court must meet?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: High quality training will ensure that alternative resolution is a realistic and cost-effective alternative to litigation.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Accreditation is offered by the Singapore Mediation Centre, Singapore International Mediation Institute and International Mediation Institute, just to name a few.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: In addition, who will be the Court-appointed mediators in the Supreme Court?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Are there plans to set up an equivalent of the State Courts' Court Dispute Resolution Cluster in the Supreme Court?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: How will the Ministry also support the growth of the private mediation service providers?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Private mediation service providers stimulate our mediation sector with innovation and competition.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: With the expanded reliance on mediation and similar processes in Singapore, we should integrate and regulate such private providers carefully.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: My third and final point is a proposal.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Today's Bill amends the law to allow various proceedings at the State Court and Supreme Court to be heard by a live video link.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: This is a welcomed move that mirrors changes which have already taken place on the ground due to COVID-19.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: However, with more proceedings taking place by live video link, there is also greater risk of issues which may undermine the security and integrity of Court proceedings.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: These include, for instance, unauthorised recording of Court proceedings, witness coaching or poor Internet connection affecting the quality of evidence presented to Court.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Such protocol should address issues from the testing of the video link to the arrangements that should be in place for witnesses to give evidence remotely.

speaker: Dr Shahira Abdullah (Nominated Member)
text: On the whole, I do support the Bill.

speaker: Dr Shahira Abdullah (Nominated Member)
text: However, I would like to bring up certain concerns and suggestions which I hope can be addressed in this debate.

speaker: Dr Shahira Abdullah (Nominated Member)
text: If this is the intention of the legislature, would educational campaigns be held to notify the general public of this substantial change in contempt laws?

speaker: Dr Shahira Abdullah (Nominated Member)
text: Could I also clarify if lawyers and litigants-in-persons will also be prohibited from making their own non-official audio transcripts of court proceedings, trials and hearings?

speaker: Dr Shahira Abdullah (Nominated Member)
text: Such recordings can facilitate understanding for proceedings that may take several days and are information intensive.

speaker: Dr Shahira Abdullah (Nominated Member)
text: Moreover, I would also like to welcome the amendments introduced under paragraph 6 through the new section 26A.

speaker: Dr Shahira Abdullah (Nominated Member)
text: The new amendments will allow for the presentation of evidence via video or television links.

speaker: Dr Shahira Abdullah (Nominated Member)
text: This will make litigation not only more efficient but cost-effective as well.

speaker: Dr Shahira Abdullah (Nominated Member)
text: Additionally, in the midst of a pandemic, this is a necessary amendment to navigate the new realities of border closures.

speaker: Dr Shahira Abdullah (Nominated Member)
text: Lay people would be unfamiliar with legal phrases that are often not used in everyday life.

speaker: Dr Shahira Abdullah (Nominated Member)
text: This move will improve the accessibility of legal due process for in-person litigants.

speaker: Dr Shahira Abdullah (Nominated Member)
text: That said, I would also like to highlight some concerns I have.

speaker: Dr Shahira Abdullah (Nominated Member)
text: There are inconsistencies in the terminology used for the civil and criminal courts and for the Singapore International Commercial Court (SICC).

speaker: Dr Shahira Abdullah (Nominated Member)
text: Moreover, these new terms do not apply to the family division of the High Court, or Family Court, or a youth court.

speaker: Dr Shahira Abdullah (Nominated Member)
text: This inconsistency may be confusing for both laypersons and lawyers and may cause both legal practitioners and laypersons to talk at cross purposes given that similar sounding words have different meanings.

speaker: Dr Shahira Abdullah (Nominated Member)
text: Also, some of the terms considered archaic and to be removed by the SICC are now used as the new simplified expressions for the civil and criminal courts.

speaker: Dr Shahira Abdullah (Nominated Member)
text: This anomaly suggests a lack of agreement by the Courts and Legislature over whether such terms are archaic or not.

speaker: Dr Shahira Abdullah (Nominated Member)
text: These include proceedings that are often personal and private in nature.

speaker: Dr Shahira Abdullah (Nominated Member)
text: For example, when would an element of public interest arise in issues of civil or family proceedings?

speaker: Dr Shahira Abdullah (Nominated Member)
text: Could the Minister also provide us with the types of scenarios contemplated that would require the exercise of the AG's new powers?

speaker: Dr Shahira Abdullah (Nominated Member)
text: The above queries are rooted in real-world concerns about the implications of the AG's new powers for parties to proceedings.

speaker: Dr Shahira Abdullah (Nominated Member)
text: Who will bear the burden of cost of the appeal if neither original party to the proceedings had sought for or wanted the appeal?

speaker: Dr Shahira Abdullah (Nominated Member)
text: Also, would the Minister be concerned about the chilling effect of these new powers on the rule of law and litigants given that, it is possible under the new laws, for almost every proceeding now to have an element of public interest?

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: The cornerstone of our legal system has always been access to justice for all.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: In pursuit of this aim, the judicial system must be constantly reviewed to remain relevant, robust and efficient.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Digital transformation and a citizenry increasingly aware of its legal rights necessitate our legal system to evolve accordingly.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: The key amendments in this Bill are in the right direction to meet these evolving trends.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: I will highlight three key areas of the amendments along with a few clarifications.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: First, I applaud the Ministry's efforts in advancing access to justice for all.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Over the years, the Ministry has simplified complex Court processes and improved accessibility to such information.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: For example, the Insolvency Office's website offers a comprehensive, one-stop suite of information for bankruptcy applications.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: The information provided on the website is reader-friendly and tailored for laypersons.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: I fully support the Ministry's move to simplify court terminology within the amendments.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: The simplification of legal terminologies is similar to those undertaken in jurisdictions, such as Britain and Canada.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Complex legal terminology in statutes can exclude the layperson from fully exercising their right of self-representation as they are less able to be cognisant of their legal rights.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: As we move towards a more accessible judicial system for litigants-in-persons, we must work towards continually revising our laws to ensure that they are easily understandable by an average layperson.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: COVID-19 has accelerated the use of technology and the Courts are now better prepared to leverage technology in legal proceedings.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Perhaps, the most important change is that of the advent of remote hearings.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: While remote hearings were practically unheard of in the justice system before the pandemic, it is now a ubiquitous feature in various jurisdictions.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: This allows the judicial system greater flexibility to dispose of matters efficiently.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Evidence may also be given via electronic means, such as live video and television links.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: This is beneficial for both the Court and litigants.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: For example, obtaining testimonies from expert witnesses, especially those of experts located out of Singapore, can be extremely costly.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: The admission of evidence via video links can significantly reduce the costs of calling upon experts.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Furthermore, with crimes and civil matters becoming increasingly borderless, witnesses may sometimes be located overseas.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: The amendments will similarly ensure that matters at hand can be disposed of expediently and reduces costs on litigants in bringing witnesses to Singapore.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Notwithstanding the benefits leveraging technology brings to the judicial system, I have one area of concern.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: As with all forms of technology, the benefits of it are followed by risks of misuse.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: My concern lies within the rising prevalence of Deepfake Artificial Intelligence.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Deepfakes are created using artificial intelligence whereby an existing image or video is manipulated and replaced with someone else's face.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: While deepfakes have been primarily contained to the manipulation of pre-recorded images and videos, there has been new software, such as Avatarify.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Unlike traditional deepfake software, it enables users to impose anyone else's face on their own in real-time within applications, such as Zoom.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: I worry that such software will become increasingly sophisticated with time.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: This increases the likelihood of manipulation during remote hearings where witnesses, or even parties, may be impersonated.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: It is thus imperative to ensure the highest level of technical standards in conducting such processes to preserve the integrity of the judicial system.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: How can video links be protected such that vulnerable persons’ identities would not be revealed via hacking?

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Lastly, on the Court’s power to order parties to attempt to resolve disputes by amicable resolution under the proposed section 23 in the Supreme Court of Judicature Act, or SCJA.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Alternative dispute resolution, or ADR, mechanisms are much more cost-effective in resolving disputes, compared to litigation.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Parties can, more often than not, reach an amicable settlement without the need to commence litigious proceedings.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: There may be situations where one or both parties do not want to participate in these ADRs in good faith.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: In such circumstances, ordering parties to do so might be counter-productive.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: At its core, the Bill modernises the form of our judicial system, while retaining its substance and core objective: accessibility to justice for all.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: I stand in support of the Bill which ensures our judicial system remains highly receptive to the needs of its users.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: I would, first, like to declare that I am a practising lawyer.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: As per the hon Justice Lee Seiu Kin in his opening speech at the launch of the Law Society’s Technology Roadshow in 2017, he shared his view that the world today is faced with "more frequent and unpredictable disruptions", and "Technology holds the promise of greater productivity and effectiveness.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: We must seize the opportunity to leverage this to higher quality legal services and cost savings for law firms, and ultimately, for the clients and society at large.” I agree wholeheartedly with his Honour.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: My speech today will, therefore, focus on the potential impact of this digital transformation and explore possible ways to utilise this transformation to reduce the costs of litigation and enhance convenience for Court users.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Over the past few years, we have begun to see a gradual modernisation of the legal industry: from law firms going paperless with the adoption of cloud-based data management systems to smaller set-up firms moving away from traditional law firm premises and towards contemporary co-working spaces, with shared meeting rooms and lounges.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: The COVID-19 pandemic has undoubtedly accelerated the pace of digital transformation.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: By now, most of the workforce, including lawyers, have become familiar with the concept of working from home in compliance with safe distancing measures.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Many client interviews as well as Court hearings are now conducted virtually, which has allowed more flexibility for lawyers in terms of their daily working schedules while managing other personal obligations.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: One of my fellow members of the Bar shared with me that she had initially thought of giving up breastfeeding her baby after returning to work from maternity leave, but she has since been able to continue doing so due to the work-from-home arrangement.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: But whilst the adoption of newer technology to conduct legal matters is the way forward, it is prudent to take heed of the downsides that come along with it as well, such as the loss of in-person communication.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Before the start of the pandemic, it was not uncommon for lawyers to bump into our peers in places such as the Court’s Bar Room or the waiting area outside the Courts’ Pre-Trial Conference chambers.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: For years, these ad hoc meetings have helped to foster the productive discussions concerning the day’s pressing agendas, or aid in the gathering of fresh perspectives on a particular subject.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: It has also served as an informal way of maintaining connections amongst those in the legal industry.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: In contrast, most correspondence these days occurs online via video-link meetings and emails, and even the actual Court hearings are isolated virtual spaces where lawyers are each segregated into their own waiting areas, unable to see or hear those who may be waiting for their own hearings to proceed.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Aside from the lack of social interaction brought about by this new norm, the rigidness of the virtual hearings has their shortcomings.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: The currently used video-link platform tends to begin its sessions without prior warning and regard for the attendee’s presence, which means that lawyers, aside from signing in for their session, do not have knowledge of the current status of the Courts, unless otherwise informed by the Court on when their hearing is likely to begin.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Worse still, in the event of delays – which may sometimes last for longer than 30 minutes at a time – the litigant-in-person or lawyer is forced to sit and wait in front of their computer at all times, unable to visit the restroom or make proper use of the downtime for other obligations.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: To address these issues, I understand from Minister’s earlier speech that features on the existing E-Litigation system will be further improvised.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: With these features, one would be able to know when their case is slated to be heard upon logging in.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: A private message function will enable users to communicate with the Court’s admin clerk on the possibility of jumping the queue due to the need to be present for another Court matter soon.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: The chat function would also allow the ability to see other counsel who may be online at the same time and to chat or start a video call with them.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: This would return some measure of communication between lawyers whereby counsel can take the opportunity while waiting, to explore settlement terms.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Although most hearings are now online affairs that require the relevant parties to attend in separate locations, many clients still prefer to do so at their lawyers’ office premises.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: This is common, particularly for the mediation sessions conducted by the Family Justice Courts, where the client still prefers the physical presence and in-person support from their lawyers to ease their anxieties.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: This arrangement is typically not a problem for medium or large-sized firms, as they have multiple meeting rooms with adequate space at their office to accommodate the lawyer and their client.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: For smaller law firms, however, the realities of limited work spaces and meeting rooms represent a significant challenge in addressing similar needs for their clients.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Over the years, I understand that the Government, along with the Law Society of Singapore, has come up with several initiatives, such as the "Tech-celerate for Law", being subsidy assistance schemes that aim to help defray costs for law practices, particularly smaller firms, and enable them to remain competitive.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: However, these schemes have so far focused mainly on helping law firms to obtain, what I would call, the “software”, such as online data management, databases and establishing online presence through marketing portals.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Parties that can benefit from the reform include those SMEs whose financial situation is affected by the pandemic; they can leverage on digital platforms to save time and money to resolve disputes.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: These improvements will be very helpful for those litigants who have financial difficulties, and victims who are wrongly accused.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: (In English): Mr Speaker, it is my opinion that in order to enhance access to justice, the relevant stakeholders will have to look into and work on the three "hows".

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: But the last point is, more often than not, the primary concern, because affordability of the costs to be incurred is often the paramount consideration for litigants when contemplating whether or not to pursue a matter further in the interest of justice.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: I am hopeful that the implementations to be rolled out subsequent to the passing of this Courts Reform Bill aims to address these points.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: However, I would like to raise three clarifications.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: There should be a clear definition of terms such that all those involved in the proceedings are clear of their meanings such that it is not open to different interpretations and, subsequently, become a point of contention in the proceedings.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: An illustration is the use of the word "claimant" instead of "plaintiff".

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: The word "claimant" is used in many contexts, such as a claimant in insurance claims or, in the US, a claimant for welfare or tax benefits. "Plaintiff" is more widely used in the Courts.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: It may be the case where it is just not possible to simplify legal terminologies and to change for the sake of accessibility may prove to be detrimental to the due process of law.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Unless the person is well-read in Singapore law and familiar with due legal processes, the desire to defend oneself in Court may, ultimately, prove detrimental.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: In the recent case of the individual publicly known as the "MBS badge lady”, the defendant's initial attempt to represent herself in Court was met with various challenges.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Subsequently, her family had to step in, engaging a lawyer to finally represent her in Court.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: While we want our legal system to be more accessible, we should also be careful not to develop the mindset of engaging legal representation only after attempts at self-representation had resulted in getting themselves into a deeper legal predicament.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Another cause for concern is the public's misunderstanding of our legal system.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: This is in light of our exposure to the American legal system and, lately, even the Korean legal system, from popular media.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Obviously, there are differences between our legal systems.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: However, members of the public sometimes misunderstand that and expect our legal proceedings to be similar.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Importantly, our changes should be recognised internationally as we are well accepted as a leading global dispute resolution hub.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: We cannot afford to make changes at the expense of the rest of the world's legal fraternity not understanding us.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: We must avoid changes that make our legal system overly localised as we are too small a country to change the norms and nomenclature of the international legal fraternity.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Lastly, while we understand the need to have remote Court hearings and sentencing during the pandemic, we must be very clear, during normal circumstances, as to when we could allow remote hearings.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: We cannot discount the fact that in some cases, it is important for the judge to be able to physically see the plaintiff or defendant and even witnesses, as it allows the judge to assess their demeanour and to see if the person is being prompted to respond.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: All these may have an impact on the eventual sentencing and, hence, should not be taken lightly.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Hence, we must be very clear as to when we can utilise remote Court hearings and not compromise the legal process for the sake of conveniences afforded by the use of technology.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: We must also be mindful to not be perceived as being too cold or inhumane when employing remote hearings.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: However, in normal circumstances, it may seem very detached and procedural for capital punishment to be meted out via Zoom.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: First, on the protocols for proceedings via video-link.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Mr Louis Ng asked whether the way that live video proceedings are conducted can be standardised.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: He mentioned the need to maintain the security and integrity of Court proceedings.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: The specific ways for participation in remote hearings are published in the Registrar's circulars and set out on the Courts' websites.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: The specific protocol that applies may vary, depending, for example, on the type of case and the litigants involved.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: On the security and integrity of proceedings, the Courts have protocols in place.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: We will take the point and emphasise this to the Courts.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Mr Murali Pillai asked how conversations between accused persons in prison and their counsel joining in from another location will be kept confidential and how accused persons will continue to have access to lawyers during remote proceedings.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: The Singapore Prison Service (SPS) has a set of purpose-built video-link facilities.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Mr Desmond Choo expressed concern with the rise of deepfake technology and the impersonation of parties or witnesses.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: The actions mentioned by Mr Choo are, of course, criminal offences.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: In terms of safeguards, the Courts are considering adopting new identification technologies.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: They are planning for them under the National Digital Identity project.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Ms Hany Soh proposed the creation of a virtual Court platform with an integrated chat function and a dynamic queue system and she explained the benefits of it.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: The Courts are working on several improvements that are aligned with Ms Soh's suggestions.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: First, there will be a new queue management system.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: It will allow the judge to re-sequence parties according to some specified criteria.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: There may also be a forecast of the number of cases which are pending, which can be made visible to all.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Second, the Courts are also enhancing the SG Courts app to allow for formal "on the record" discussions between lawyers and the Court.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Ms Soh has also asked about assistance schemes for smaller law firms to defray the cost of purchasing virtual hearing equipment.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: She has also asked whether filing fees can be reviewed and whether the Courts are able to provide more spaces for practitioners to communicate with their clients in-person.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: She did mention that MinLaw has been working on initiatives to help law firms, especially the smaller ones, ramp up their use of technology.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: These efforts include Tech-celerate for Law and Tech Start for Law, as Ms Soh has pointed out.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: We will build on these to further help law firms adopt technology and transit to remote hearings.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: This will also help with their transition onto the electronic Court systems.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Major initiatives that law firms can look forward to will be a Legal Tech Platform which will enable, in an affordable way, law practices and lawyers to work anytime, anywhere.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: This is a matters management tool designed specifically around legal workflows.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: We aim to integrate the platform with commonly used technology solutions like practice management solutions, document management solutions, communication tools like WhatsApp and Microsoft Teams and Government systems like LawNet, eLitigation and ACRA that lawyers commonly interact with.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: We are also putting together an Industry Digital Plan, which will provide a step-by-step guide for lawyers to assess their own digital readiness and provide information on the technology solutions commonly used by lawyers, which will be mapped to different stages of digital maturity.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: The industry digital plan will be launched in tandem with the legal technology platform.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: On Ms Hany Soh's question about defraying hardware costs, generally, the Government does not favour any particular group, say, lawyers and so on, to buy equipment for their practices.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: On the provision of physical space, there are already many spaces within existing courthouses which lawyers can utilise to meet with their clients.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: We will pass the feedback onto the Courts.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Moving on to paper hearings, Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim sought clarifications on paper hearings.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: First, whether parties can opt in for paper hearings.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: If parties prefer the matter to be heard on paper, they can inform the Court.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: The Court, ultimately, has the final say but it will take this into account when considering whether to proceed with a paper hearing.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: It, obviously, saves costs and time, provided the matter can be dealt with through a paper hearing.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Third, Mr Zhulkarnain asked whether there can be a fast track for the case management of paper hearings.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: That, really, has got to depend on each case, its nature, complexity and how prepared parties are for a speedier management of the case.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Fourth, Mr Zhulkarnain asked about paper hearings in criminal proceedings.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: In the context of remote hearings, Mr Sharael Taha also underscored the need to be mindful of the human aspect in criminal matters.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: The Courts will exercise the discretion to conduct paper or asynchronous hearings judiciously.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Mr Murali Pillai also raised a query on how the Courts will ensure that litigants-in-persons (LIPs) are not disadvantaged by remote or paper hearings.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: LIPs who have concerns with using remote technology or with a paper hearing can notify the Courts.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: LIPs will be encouraged to take advantage of remote or paper hearing processes but, ultimately, it is an option for them.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: If a litigant does not have the equipment or Internet connectivity, he can, of course, come to Court to use in-Court facilities that do cater for remote hearings.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: The Courts have published detailed guidelines on the conduct of remote hearings.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Users may also reach out to the Courts to get help.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Dr Shahira Abdullah mentioned that under the amendments to the Administration of Justice Protection Act, litigants and lawyers will now be prohibited from making their own non-official audio transcripts of Court proceedings.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: The amendments under this Bill do not change the underlying position today.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: The amendments simply update the provisions so that unauthorised recordings of remote Court proceedings will likewise be in contempt.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Mr Louis Ng asked a number of questions.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: One, on the scope of the Court's powers to order parties to attempt amicable resolution.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: An attempt at amicable resolution may be appropriate where strict legal remedies may not necessarily address the underlying concerns and interests of parties or where litigation is not cost effective.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Second, where parties have gone through formal processes, such as mediation, neutral evaluation, settlement negotiations with exchange of draft settlement agreements, these are all likely to constitute clear attempts at amicable resolution.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Third, Mr Louis Ng asked how the Court will ensure that parties will make good faith attempts at amicable resolution and what would be the consequences of non-compliance with the Court's direction to attempt such amicable resolution.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Mr Desmond Choo also sought clarification on whether the Court will consider the intentions of the parties before exercising the powers.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: The short answer to Mr Louis Ng's question is that it is not easy to ensure good faith negotiations.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: But in deciding whether to order parties to attempt amicable resolution, the Courts will take into account all the facts before them, including whether any of the parties have refused to attempt to resolve the dispute by amicable resolution, and why.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Where necessary, the Courts may require the parties or their counsel to explain why the matter cannot be settled amicably.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Mr Louis Ng asked whether Registrars will be required to undergo training in mediation and other alternative dispute resolution processes (ADR), and whether there will be a minimum requirement that must be met and who the Court-appointed mediators will be.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: In the State Courts, mediation may be conducted by specially-trained District Judges or Court Volunteer Mediators.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: They have extensive experience in mediation and other ADR processes, and they undergo continuous training in ADR.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Alternatively, they should minimally hold a Level 3 qualification as a Singapore International Mediation Institute Accredited Mediator.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: For the Supreme Court, a Registrar conducting ADR, or a Court-appointed mediator, will similarly be trained in the particular ADR processes.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Mr Louis Ng asked if there are plans to set up an equivalent of the State Courts' Court Dispute Resolution Cluster in the Supreme Court.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Lastly, on Mr Louis Ng's question on how MinLaw supports the growth of private mediation service providers, MinLaw's role is to ensure a conducive environment for our dispute resolution ecosystem to thrive.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: We work closely with mediation service providers, such as Singapore Mediation Centre (SMC), Singapore International Mediation Centre (SIMC) and so on, to ensure that their service offerings address the different user needs and complement the Court-based dispute resolution mechanisms.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: We also have the Singapore International Mediation Institute (SIMI).

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: It looks at accreditation and mediation standards to support professionalising mediation.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim asked about security for costs in the context of an application for freestanding interim relief.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: A defendant may apply for security for the defendant's costs of the action, on the basis that the applicant has no nexus or assets in Singapore.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: On vessel arrests, these fall outside the scope of freestanding interim relief that the General Division can grant.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Mr Zhulkarnain sought clarification regarding the Singapore International Commercial Court (SICC)'s jurisdiction.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: He asked when the action, and the counterclaim taken as a whole, would still maintain an international and commercial character.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: The assessment cannot be a purely quantitative one.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: The Court will have to consider all the relevant facts and circumstances, assess whether the counterclaim, third-party proceedings change the nature or substance of the action in such a way that the action, seen as a whole, no longer maintains an international or commercial nature.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Mr Zhulkarnain also asked about the consolidation of proceedings under SICC and whether similar considerations would apply if one proceeding is in a different Court from SICC.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: The consolidation of proceedings under SICC may require different considerations, as parties would have already commenced separate proceedings.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: If proceedings are not before the same Court, but a party believes that an application for consolidation is necessary, then a transfer application should be taken out to bring the proceedings before the same Court, before applying for any consolidation.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: There are rules on how that takes place.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: But, of course, the requirements for proper service on that party will still apply.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: As with any judgment of the General Division of the High Court, an SICC judgment is likely to be enforceable in major commercial jurisdiction and many other regional ones.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: There are standard laws on how this takes place.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Mr Pritam Singh, Ms Shahira Abdullah, Mr Zhulkarnain and Mr Murali Pillai have raised a number of queries regarding the Attorney-General (AG)'s right to intervene.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: First, as my colleague Minister Edwin Tong mentioned in Parliament yesterday, the statutory framework is based on the established role of the AG.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: He is the Guardian of the public interest.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: This has been recognised by our Courts as well as by Members who have spoken on this Bill and previously.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: The proposed amendments are consistent with that principle.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: The Court of Appeal, for example, has noted that the AG intervenes on a non-partisan basis.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: He is disinterested in the interests of the parties to the litigation.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: The issues that he raises most logically, must have a discernible impact beyond the specific parties and the specific dispute before the Court.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Second, it is important to understand the context in which this proposal arises.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Let us say you have a civil case between two parties.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Prima facie, nothing to do with the state, or the public.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: But in the course of the dispute or from the pleadings, or in the course of the arguments, issues arise which, potentially, are detrimental to the public interest.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
