text: But the test that is laid out by the Courts on what amounts to negligence will impact on future claims on the basis of medical negligence.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: So, it will impact both patients and doctors, and they cannot come forward and intervene in this case.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: The only party who can do so in the public interest is the AG.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: So, this relates to the provision of medical advice.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: To take another example, the AG has intervened on the nature and scope of professional and ethical duties.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: For example, in Deepak Sharma v Law Society of Singapore, on what duties are owed by lawyers in making claims for costs.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: In such cases, it is sensible, obvious, that the AG must have a right to intervene, to protect the public interest and put forward arguments.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: The AG's presence assists the Court and also informs the Court of the possible broader implications on the public interest.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Third, the AG's application to intervene is only an intermediate step in the dispute.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: At the first stage, the Court will check to ensure that the AG has set out adequate details, the basis, grounds for his request to be added as a party.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Only if the Court is satisfied that the AG has explained the reasons for his intervention sufficiently, then the Court will grant permission for the AG to intervene.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: If anyone wishes to oppose the AG's intervention, then they may apply to set aside the Court's permission.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: This brings us to the second stage, which will involve the AG and the other parties, because the first stage is ex parte.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: At this stage, the parties can raise any concerns they might have about the AG's addition to the proceedings.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: If any party objects to the intervention, the Court will assess whether the permission that has been granted to the AG should now be reversed.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: The Court's assessment will be made based on the interests of justice.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: It can take into account and balance various considerations, including the possible inconvenience, costs to a party, if AG is added; and the potential benefits if AG is allowed to join the proceedings, to add his perspectives on the matter.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Any Court will proceed on the basis that the AG is a Guardian of the public interest, and if he comes to Court and says there is an important matter of public interest here, it is, generally, not assumed that the AG is being frivolous.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: There must be a serious point and it is a matter of public interest.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: When someone comes in, particularly the AG, to put forward the arguments, the Court knows that it will be of tremendous assistance to the Court.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Ultimately, how it decides is for the Court, but the Court gets tremendous assistance from the AG.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Mr Pritam Singh asked if this is a shift in the common law position.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: He has asked why not we just stick with the existing position, why do we need a new framework.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: The common law position does allow AG to intervene.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: For example, in the case of ARW v Comptroller of Income Tax, the Appellant was a private company, which applied for specific discovery of internal documents belonging to IRAS.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: So, this is a taxpayer, I believe, who sought documents from IRAS, but it goes beyond that to a broader principle of when you can apply for documents against a Government agency.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Whether it should be allowed or it should not be allowed is a matter for the Court.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Whether such a principle should apply to all public departments in the context of a private civil dispute, albeit against IRAS, is a matter of public interest.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: The AG should be entitled to put forward his position why it is or it is not in the public interest to make a particular order.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: And that is for the Courts to decide.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: So, the AG applied to intervene to make representations on the issue of public interest privilege under the Evidence Act.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Application for intervention was filed in the High Court.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: There was dispute on the addition of the AG to the proceedings.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: It was resolved by the Court of Appeal 20 months later.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: All that is good, but 20 months have been lost.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Taking into account what the Court of Appeal had said and the fact that you do not want these things to be unnecessarily delayed, I will say this to Members.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: As in the cases cited, parties to civil litigation are often seeking to interpret the rules in their own favour.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: If they succeed, sometimes, it is the man in the street who will pay the bill, ultimately, if it is against the public interest.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: As I have said, the addition of AG to the proceedings is a procedural step.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: It does not mean that either of the original parties has somehow "lost" or "won" the original lawsuit, though I can understand, they may not like what the AG is going to say.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: In that sense, they would prefer if the AG is not present, but that is not the way hearings and arguments should go.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Mr Pritam Singh has cited various statutes which expressly provide for the AG's right to intervene: Charities Act, Industrial Relations Act.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: In those pieces of legislation, the AG has an unqualified entitlement to intervene in the specified categories of proceedings.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Here, the proposal is that even the addition itself, the parties can oppose if they wish; then, the Court has got to decide after hearing both sides.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Mr Murali Pillai had a suggestion that the AG's role as Guardian of the public interest be codified in the Constitution.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: As mentioned, the AG's role as Guardian of the public interest has been affirmed by the Court of Appeal in a number of cases.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: It has also been recognised by this House yesterday by Mr Murali Pillai and Mr Pritam Singh.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Mr Pritam Singh asked if the amendments are intended as a contingency or whether there are new areas of public interest that the Government is concerned about.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: I am not sure what Mr Pritam Singh is concerned about; or that we always think ahead and are planning something else that he is concerned about.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: But it is not going to be possible to predict how other areas of laws in which such interventions may be required in the future, might take place.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: And what questions of public interest may arise, will depend on the facts and circumstances of each case.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Mr Zhulkarnain also asked whether there will still be a need for AG to intervene if a party to the proceedings can put forth an opposing view to the Court.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: The AG's role is not to put forward supporting or opposing views but to represent the public interest and what, in his view, is best stated in terms of the public interest, whereas the views of parties to the proceedings will obviously be influenced by their respective interests.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: And, sometimes, there cannot be a substitute for the non-partisan views of the AG.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: The parties to a civil litigation are not there to advance public interest.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: They are there to advance or forward their own case.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Sometimes, it is necessary that somebody else is there to protect the public interest.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Mr Zhulkarnain also asked whether the Court can instead invite the AG to make submissions as an independent counsel under the Legal Profession Act.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: The role of an independent counsel is to address the Court on specific issues of law, at the invitation of the Court.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Whereas the AG's submissions on issues of public interest may well go beyond specific issues of law.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Unlike an independent counsel, the AG will be deemed a party to the proceedings if he is added on.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: And when he intervenes as Guardian of the public interest, like other parties, he will be able to make applications, file affidavits and will also have the right of appeal.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Mr Murali Pillai asked whether the AG has a duty of full and frank disclosure, since he will be making an ex parte application when applying for permission of the Court to intervene.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Dr Shahira asked who should bear the costs where the parties choose not to appeal the Court's decision but the AG decides to do so.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Mr Sharael Taha and Dr Shahira spoke in support of the terminology amendments.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Laws must be clear and easy to understand.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Dr Shahira had highlighted the differences in terminology amendments that will apply across the Courts and said that this might cause confusion.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: For the Family Justice Courts (FJC), the rules are being reviewed and will be revamped in due course.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: However, because of the unique nature of family proceedings, some terminology amendments will be specific to the FJC.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: For example, the terminology of parties in a divorce.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: The naming of parties as "applicants" and "respondents" is intended to avoid calling them "claimants" and "defendants".

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Calling someone a "defendant" sometimes could be seen as pejorative.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: So, this is really in line with FJC's move towards therapeutic justice.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: For the Singapore International Commercial Court (SICC), the differences are relatively limited.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: These differences arise as a result of the differences in Court procedure in SICC and the General Division.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: The procedure in SICC is specifically tailored to facilitate international commercial litigation.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: We, therefore, do not think that this will give rise to confusion since the respective rules of Court will make clear the procedures that should be used.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: On legal representation, public education, building a world-class legal system raised by Mr Sharael Taha, these are issues which my Ministry is working on.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: And I would say our legal system is, generally, highly regarded.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: That, Sir, brings me to the end of my responses to the questions raised.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: I believe I have answered all the questions raised by Members.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: And with that, I beg to move, Sir.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: My fundamental interest was to try and understand whether the common law position would change with regard to the two-stage process.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: I listened very carefully to Minister Edwin Tong's speech at the Second Reading and when Minister Edwin Tong went through the various clauses that pertain to Part 4 of the Bill, insofar as Part 4 section 4A(4) was concerned, it reads in the Explanatory Statement: "In considering whether to grant permission to intervene, the Court need only be satisfied that the grounds for intervention are adequately set out in the affidavit.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: The Court is not to examine the merits of those grounds." But the Minister added in his speech the words "at that stage", and my concerns about at what point the merits of the AG's arguments would be assessed by the Court is the subject matter of my query.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: For example, at paragraph 56 of Deepak Sharma v Law Society of Singapore, the Court of Appeal noted that if the Court takes the view that the issues that the AG raised do not pertain to the public interest, it is open to the Court to refuse a cost order in favour of the AG, even if the AG considers his intervention and submissions were warranted in the public interest.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Although this point pertains to costs and not the subject of an order to set aside the order for the AG to intervene as envisaged by clause 488, is it not incongruous for the Court to consider the public interest rationale for the AG's grounds for intervention at one stage of the proceedings, but not at the point of application of leave to intervene as it is the case under the common law today?

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: There is an expectation that you can assess the public interest grounds when you look at costs but, earlier on, for example, an opposing party applies to intervene to challenge the entry of the AG, the Court cannot look into the merits of public interest grounds.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: So, my suggestion, number one, is that, is that not incongruous?

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: To further this point, and I agree with the Minister, AG is to act in a non-partisan way and that is the expectation and it is important that we record that in the Hansard.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: But in Deepak Sharma v Law Society of Singapore, the Court of Appeal also notes the prospect of an adverse Court order against the AG.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: And there, the Court says, "in cases where the AG has intervened with improper motives such as to deliberately advance the interests of one of the parties to litigation, that would take the AG out of his capacity as a non-partisan advocate of the public interest and into the shoes of a de facto party to the litigation." This again aligns with the earlier question I had.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: If the prospect of an AG acting in a partisan manner can be contemplated at one stage of the proceedings – this is the determination of costs – would the Minister not agree that the Courts should be empowered to consider the public interest grounds at the point of the AG's intervention in proceedings?

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: I think both questions actually come back to one: is it two stages?

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: When there is an ex parte application, the Courts hear the party making the ex parte application.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: And if, on the face of it, it is completely clear that there is no basis, then they will throw it out.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: But when it moves on to the substantive hearing, these issues will arise in much greater detail.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: And that is when the Court then goes into it in-depth.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: But I think this is fairly standard, it happens all the time.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: For example, the parties can, as I have said, oppose the AG having been added.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: And they can raise a number of grounds for the AG having been added.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: After the AG has been added ex parte, the parties can oppose that procedure and the process.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The Court will then consider if such an application is made.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: If the Court confirms that the AG has been rightly added, then the next step is to deal with the substantive issues, the point or principle that AG makes and how it impacts one or the other parties' arguments or the outcome itself.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: I understand the parties can oppose the ex parte application.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: When the ex parte application is made, the Court makes the order for the AG to be added but the parties can then subsequently say, that should not have been done.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: So, at the stage where the party says that should not have been done, what the Bill does is to confirm that the Court cannot look into the public interest ground in assessing that application.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: It should be dealt with on the more substantive points.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: If, subsequently, the Court finds that the AG case has got no basis or he contributed in the ways that the Courts have identified in very, very narrow categories, they have powers to deal with it.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: I just have one clarification in respect of the documents-only hearing.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: I agree that it depends on the case and, especially given our current context of a docket system, whether there would be an internal tendency to decide on documents only hearing at the earliest possible opportunity, so that we can save much time and cost for the cases.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: It is difficult for me to set it out in broad terms today.      .

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: As the amendments are related, may I seek your permission to move them together?

speaker: The Chairman
text: Consequent amendments* to be made will be made.
